processing: Grown and made in Wuyi as a rock tea: shaken, partly oxidised, rolled and roasted. Roast level varies by maker.
harvest_season: Spring, as is usual for Wuyi rock teas.
appearance_dry: Typical of Wuyi rock teas: dark, twisted strips.
appearance_liquor: Typical of roasted Wuyi oolongs: clear orange-gold to amber.
appearance_wet: Typical of the class: green-brown leaves with darker edges.
taste_profile: Not well recorded in the sources checked. Its use as a named aroma cultivar points to a floral lift; expect that over the roast and mineral weight typical of the class.

brewing.notes: The usual approach for Wuyi rock teas. Keep early steeps short and do not lift the lid too late, or the aroma flattens.

vintage_note: Sold by spring harvest year and roast, like other Wuyi rock teas. Look for the number 305 as well as the name.
description:
Rui Xiang is a modern bred cultivar, known in the trade by its number, 305, and grown in Wuyi.

In Wuyi it is made as a rock tea, with shaking, partial oxidation and a roast.

The tasting record checked here is thin, so expect the broad pattern of the class with some floral lift. Keep early steeps short.

When buying, ask for the year, the roast and where it grew.
history: Rui Xiang is a recent cultivar, listed under code 305 with Huang Jin Gui (Huangdan) as parent and a publication year of 2003. The same list traces this series of numbered varieties to the Fujian Tea Research Institute.
